newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin "ready for battle" as returns to Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin "ready for battle" as returns to Kremlin.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin was back in the Kremlin on Monday, seven weeks after a multiple heart bypass gave him a new lease on life, and the 65-year-old president said he was "ready for battle".

At what is effectively the start of a new term of office -- six months late -- Yeltsin promised Russians better fortune in the New Year. Though thinner and looking fitter than before the operation, he showed little of the combative fire that won him re-election last July against a stiff communist challenge.
Asked whether life would get better for Russians next year after five years of post-Soviet chaos and decline, the president replied simply: "Absolutely, absolutely."
Official data released on Monday showed gross domestic product (GDP) shrank another six percent in 1996, confounding more optimistic forecasts made at the start of the year.
Social problems have intensified since Yeltsin dropped out of sight a few days before his July 3 re-election victory. His defeated communist rival heaped scorn on the president's return.
"Yeltsin is in no condition to resolve even a single issue facing Russia today," Gennady Zyuganov told a news conference.

Wrapped up against the sub-zero temperature, Yeltsin spoke only briefly with a camera crew as he stepped from his car, telling them he was feeling fine and that his priorities would include wage and pension arrears and military reform.
Millions of state and private-sector workers have not been paid for months, leaving much of the population on the breadline and provoking sporadic strikes across the country.

Discreet jockeying for position among Kremlin aides broke into open conflict after Yeltin, clearly very ill, went on television in early September to say that only surgery could spare him from a twilight existence of chronic heart problems.
Shortly before the November 5 operation to bypass clogged cardiac arteries, Yeltsin had to sack security adviser Alexander Lebed amid charges of plots and counter-plots.
The president met one of Lebed's main rivals, chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, on Monday to go over the political situation.
In an apparent vote of confidence in Chubais, Yeltsin's spokesman told Itar-Tass news agency the president was "pleased" with the work of the Kremlin administration during his absence.

Yeltsin, who will meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday, also spoke to British Prime Minister John Major by telephone and invited him to Russia next year. The president already has plans to meet the U.S., German and French leaders.
His more pressing domestic business includes a round of elections for regional governors and next month's voting in Chechnya, where violence rocked a fragile ceasefire last week.

Kremlin candidates took a narrow lead in Sunday's batch of elections, though Zyuganov claimed success for the opposition. It already controls the State Duma lower house of parliament and regional victories would increase its weight in the upper house.
Chubais, a particular hate figure for communists, aims to avert that by drawing new communist-backed governors, who sit in the Federation Council upper house, into the Kremlin's sphere.

Michael DeBakey, the veteran Texas heart specialist who advised on his operation, told BBC radio that Yeltsin would have no trouble working eight hours a day at this stage, although it would be another month or so before he was back to full health.

Asked about speculation from opponents that the president had started drinking again, DeBakey said the odd tipple would do him no harm. But he voiced concern that the Russian habit of repeated toasts during festive meals was a recipe for trouble.
